scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Rhythm of the Fields
This is Pungmul. Ancient to present.
on_screen: Title card: Pungmul · South Korea · Ancient to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pungmul originated in agrarian labor and shamanistic rituals.
It was suppressed during the Japanese colonial era (1910–1945) under the label 'nongak'.
In 1978, Kim Duk-soo and Kim Yong-bae developed 'SamulNori', a seated, stage-oriented version of the tradition, which revitalized interest in the genre.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically used for farming labor, village rituals, and exorcising demons.
In the 1970s and 80s, it became a symbol of political protest and community mobilization.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Samulnori. Musiche e danze della Corea, compagnia PUNG-MU-AK: 6 novembre 2000 - Arena del Sole (https://archive.org/details/20001106.samulnori)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performers move in processions or circular formations.
'Wit-Noleum' (upper performance) involves head and ribbon movements, while 'Bal-Noleum' (footwork) provides the base.
Dancers use the sogo drum to punctuate movement.
Watch for Sangmonori, Jinpuri.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Outdoor processions or circular formations (jinpuri).

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The ensemble features the kkwaenggwari (lead gong), janggu (hourglass drum), buk (barrel drum), and jing (gong).
The taepyeongso (wind instrument) often provides melodic accompaniment.
Listen for the kkwaenggwari, janggu, buk, jing.
The pulse is Variable (e.g., 12/8, 9/8, 4/4).
A dense, polyrhythmic texture dominated by metallic gong strikes and deep drum thuds, punctuated by the high-pitched, piercing melody of the taepyeongso.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear traditional 'minbok' clothing.
Headgear includes the 'gokkal' (floral hat) or the 'sangmo' (ribbon-hat).
Performances typically occur outdoors, though modern 'SamulNori' is performed seated on stage.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Kim Duk-soo, Kim Yong-bae, Sim U-seong, Yi Jong-hun.
Five major styles: Jinju Samcheonpo (Yeongnam), Pyeongtaek (Utdari), Iri (Honam Udo), Gangneung (Yeongdong), and Imsil Pilbong (Honam Jwado).
Derived from ancient shamanistic rituals and Namsadang itinerant troupes; influenced the modern SamulNori genre.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Pungmul is child of SamulNori: A staged, seated percussion genre derived from Pungmul.
Pungmul is parent of Namsadang: Itinerant troupes that historically maintained the Pungmul repertoire.
Pungmul is variant of Pung cholom: A similar dance from Manipur, India.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Pungmul has roots in shamanistic rituals intended to bless villages, fields, and homes; some performances remain tied to these spiritual contexts.
